## Overview

This note introduces homogeneous polynomials and the basic definition
of Lorentzian polynomials.

::: {.callout-note}
## Main goal

Understand how the Hessian signature condition controls the coefficients
of a homogeneous polynomial.
:::

## Definition

::: {#def-homogeneous}

## Homogeneous polynomial

A polynomial \(f\in \mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is homogeneous of
degree \(d\) if

\[
f(\lambda x_1,\ldots,\lambda x_n)
=
\lambda^d f(x_1,\ldots,x_n)
\]

for every \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\).

:::

We will use @def-homogeneous throughout these notes.

## An important formula

Let

\[
f(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in\Delta_n^d}c_\alpha x^\alpha,
\qquad
\Delta_n^d=
\left\{
\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^n:
\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i=d
\right\}.
\] {#eq-polynomial}

Equation @eq-polynomial gives the coefficient representation of \(f\).

## Theorem

::: {#thm-euler}

## Euler's homogeneous function identity

If \(f\) is homogeneous of degree \(d\), then

\[
\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}
=
df.
\]

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## Show proof

Differentiate

\[
f(\lambda x)=\lambda^d f(x)
\]

with respect to \(\lambda\), and then substitute \(\lambda=1\).

:::

## Example

::: {#exm-quadratic}

## A quadratic example

Consider

\[
f(x,y,z)=xy+xz+yz.
\]

Its Hessian matrix is

\[
\nabla^2f=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1&1\\
1&0&1\\
1&1&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The eigenvalues are \(2,-1,-1\), so it has exactly one positive
eigenvalue.

:::

::: {.callout-warning}

## Common mistake

The Hessian condition alone is not always sufficient. One must also
check the support and coefficient conditions appearing in the
definition being used.

:::
